To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the transverse-mass spectra are well described in wide ranges of the incident energies, rapidity bins and centralities of heavy-ion collisions.

the transverse-mass spectra are determined by the collective expansion of the system and its dynamical freezeout, and the dynamical freezeout is determined by the competition of the collective expansion with the deceleration of the particles due to the interaction with other particles in the system.
the spectra of all particles produced in heavy-ion collisions are well described within the framework of the model of three fluid dynamics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of transverse-mass spectra in heavy-ion collisions in the framework of three-fluid hydrodynamics.
the study of collective phenomena in high-energy heavy-ion collisions.

the following problems: (i) the transverse-mass spectra in the central collisions at the highest RHIC and LHC energies, and the spectra in the most peripheral collisions; (ii) the transverse mass spectra in the intermediate rapidity range; (iii) the spectra at the incident energies 4A Gev < or approx. 160A GeV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the three-fluid model is a reliable and predictive model of heavy-ion collisions.
the model of three- fluid dynamics is able to describe the transverse-mass spectra in heavy-ion collisions in the whole range of the incident energies and rapidities.
the hydrodynamic expansion is a key factor in the formation of collective flow in high-energy heavy-ion collisions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the model of three fluids is capable to explain a wide variety of observables in heavy-ion collisions, from the initial stage to the final state, in a consistent way.
a hydrodynamic model of the system is able to reproduce the transverse-mass spectra in wide ranges.
the transverse-mass spectra in heavy-ion collisions at energies E{sub lab}< or approx. 160 GeV/nucleon are determined by the collective expansion of the system and by its dynamical freeze out.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hydrodynamic evolution of the system is important even at very low collision energies, and it should be taken into account in any theoretical analysis of the data.
the transverse-mass spectra are determined by the freeze-out conditions of the system, which are different at different collision energies.
the transverse-mass spectra in heavy-ion collisions at energies 2-160A GeV are dominated by the hydrodynamic expansion of hot and dense matter.
